builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
summary: It replaces content-based filters and LLM-as-a-judge screening of fine-tuning data with gradient attribution that flags benign-looking examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. It costs backpropagation through the final four transformer blocks per example plus storage of gradient embeddings for the full dataset, which is feasible on a single GPU but adds a preprocessing pipeline and requires access to unsafe-response reference data. It can fail when the proxy unsafe behaviors used for alignment do not match the attack distribution the deployment actually faces, when the removal fraction trades off capability on narrower datasets, or when safety degradation stems from effects gradient alignment does not capture.
rationale: The method runs on a single GPU at million-example scale and directly serves teams that fine-tune open models on third-party instruction data, but the 22% attack-reduction claim should be validated against the reader's own model, data mix, and threat model before adoption.
technique: Gradient-based filtering of safety-degrading fine-tuning data

claims.statement: It replaces content-based filters and LLM-as-a-judge screening of fine-tuning data with gradient attribution that flags benign-looking examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. It costs backpropagation through the final four transformer blocks per example plus storage of gradient embeddings for the full dataset, which is feasible on a single GPU but adds a preprocessing pipeline and requires access to unsafe-response reference data. It can fail when the proxy unsafe behaviors used for alignment do not match the attack distribution the deployment actually faces, when the removal fraction trades off capability on narrower datasets, or when safety degradation stems from effects gradient alignment does not capture.

Training on SafeTulu (Tulu 3 with the top 20% of gradient-aligned examples removed) reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, with capability largely preserved; attribution AUC reaches 0.865 on emergent misalignment.
